questions.stem: John works in a cake shop. He records which of the five most popular cakes each customer buys. What type of data is this?
questions.hint: Ask: are the categories names with no natural order, or numbers?

steps.explain: The data records a cake *name* (a category), not a number, so it is categorical rather than quantitative.
The five cake types have no natural ranking or order (e.g. "chocolate" is not "more" or "less" than "vanilla"), so it is nominal rather than ordinal.

questions.stem: The Pareto chart below shows the number of orders received each month (bars) and the cumulative percentage of orders (line). What percentage of orders were received in May?
questions.hint: May's own share is the *difference* between the cumulative % up to May and the cumulative % up to April.

steps.explain: The cumulative % line reaches 50% after April and 70% after May, so May alone contributed the gap between these two readings.
Checking directly from the bar heights confirms this: May had 9 orders out of \(25+9+7.5+5+2.5=49\) total orders.
The bar-height calculation is the precise one — May accounts for 18% of total orders.

questions.stem: A sample of 14 people were asked how many hours of television they watched the previous night. The results are shown in the dot plot below. Find the mean and sample standard deviation of these times, correct to one decimal place.

steps.explain: Read the frequencies directly from the dot plot: \(x=0\) has 3 dots, \(x=1\) has 2, \(x=2\) has 4, \(x=3\) has 2, \(x=4\) has 2, \(x=5\) has 1 (total \(3+2+4+2+2+1=14\), matching the sample size).
Convert each frequency to a probability (proportion) by dividing by 14, then compute the mean \(\bar x = \sum x\cdot p\).
Evaluate the sum.
For the sample standard deviation, first find \(E(X^2)\), then use \(s = \sqrt{E(X^2)-\bar x^2}\) (using calculator statistics mode for the sample SD directly is equally valid).
Substitute into the standard deviation formula and evaluate.
State both final answers, rounded to 1 decimal place.

questions.stem: Which statement is true for an ungrouped data set with no outliers?
options: The largest possible range is 5 times the interquartile range.
The largest possible range is 3 times the interquartile range.
The largest possible range is 4 times the interquartile range.
The largest possible range is 2 times the interquartile range.
questions.hint: A value is an outlier if it lies more than \(1.5 \times \text{IQR}\) beyond \(Q_1\) or \(Q_3\) — with no outliers, the most extreme values sit right at that boundary.

steps.explain: With no outliers, the minimum and maximum values can each be at most \(1.5\,\text{IQR}\) away from \(Q_1\) and \(Q_3\) respectively (any further and they would be outliers).
The range spans from the minimum to the maximum, which is the IQR itself plus the two 1.5-IQR margins on either side.
Add the three portions together.

questions.stem: The scatterplot shows the relationship between expenditure per primary school student (as a % of GDP) and life expectancy (years) for 15 countries. The lower quartile of expenditure is \(Q_L=8.4\) and upper quartile \(Q_U=22.5\).

parts.stem: (a) What is the interquartile range for the expenditure data?
parts.hint: IQR \(= Q_U - Q_L\).

steps.explain: Subtract the lower quartile from the upper quartile.
Evaluate.

parts.stem: (b) Another country has an expenditure of 47.6% of GDP. Would this country be an outlier for this data set?
options: No, since 47.6 is close to the other high values
parts.hint: A value is an outlier if it lies beyond \(Q_U+1.5\times\text{IQR}\) (or below \(Q_L-1.5\times\text{IQR}\)).

steps.explain: Calculate the outlier boundary above \(Q_U\), using the IQR found in part (a).
Compare the new country's value to this boundary.
Since the value exceeds the outlier boundary, it is classified as an outlier.

parts.stem: (d) Using the least-squares line \(y=1.29x+49.9\), estimate the life expectancy in a country with an expenditure of 18% of GDP.
parts.hint: Substitute \(x=18\) into the given regression line.

steps.explain: Substitute \(x=18\) into the regression equation.
Evaluate.
Round appropriately (reading directly from the graph, values between 72-74 are all acceptable).

parts.stem: (e) Why is this line NOT useful for predicting life expectancy in a country with an expenditure of 60% of its GDP?

steps.explain: Substitute \(x=60\) into the regression line to see what it predicts.
This predicted life expectancy (over 100 years) far exceeds any realistic human life expectancy, and 60% of GDP is well outside the range of the original data (5%-27.5%).
steps.work: Predicted \(y>100\), unrealistic; \(x=60\) is outside the observed data range

steps.explain: This is extrapolation — using the line far beyond the range it was fitted to — which is not a reliable prediction method.
steps.work: \(\therefore\) the line is only reliable (predictive) within the range of the original data, not for extrapolated values like 60% GDP.

Milo’s upper half and upper whisker are much longer, indicating positive (right) skew. Aurora’s five-number summary is approximately balanced around its median.
steps.work: Milo: positive skew; Aurora: approximately symmetric

steps.explain: The higher median supports Aurora’s claim about typical results.
steps.work: \(\boxed{\text{Yes, Aurora’s results were better by median}}\)

questions.stem: A set of data has a lower quartile (Q_L) of 24 and an upper quartile (Q_U) of 42. What is the maximum possible range for this set of data if there are no outliers?
questions.hint: Use the 1.5×IQR outlier fences as the furthest possible minimum and maximum values.

parts.stem: A set of data has lower quartile Q_L=24 and upper quartile Q_U=42. What is the maximum possible range if there are no outliers?
parts.hint: Find IQR. The no-outlier fences are QL−1.5IQR and QU+1.5IQR.

steps.explain: Calculate the interquartile range.
With no outliers, the data can extend down to the lower fence and up to the upper fence.
The largest possible range is upper fence minus lower fence.

questions.stem: A school collected data related to the reasons given by students for arriving late. The Pareto chart shows the data collected. What percentage of students gave the reason “Train or bus delay”?
questions.hint: A percentage is the category frequency divided by the total frequency, multiplied by 100.

parts.stem: The Pareto chart shows reasons students gave for arriving late. What percentage of students gave “Train or bus delay”?
parts.hint: Use the frequency bar for train/bus delay divided by the total number of students, then convert to a percentage.

steps.explain: Read the train/bus delay frequency from the chart and compare it with the total across all categories.
The train/bus bar is about 30 students out of about 500 total.
So the answer is 6%.

questions.stem: The heights, in centimetres, of 10 players on a basketball team are shown: 170, 180, 185, 188, 192, 193, 193, 194, 196, 202. Is the height of the shortest player on the team considered an outlier? Justify your answer with calculations.
questions.hint: Use the median of each half of the ordered data to find the quartiles, then calculate the lower outlier fence.

parts.stem: The heights of 10 basketball players are 170, 180, 185, 188, 192, 193, 193, 194, 196, 202 cm. Is the height of the shortest player an outlier? Justify with calculations.
options: Yes; 170 cm is below the lower fence 171.5 cm
No; the lower fence is 160 cm
parts.hint: Find Q1 and Q3 from the lower and upper halves, then apply the lower 1.5×IQR fence.

steps.explain: Split the ordered ten values into two groups of five. Q1 is the middle of the lower group; Q3 is the middle of the upper group.
Calculate IQR and the lower fence.
The minimum 170 is below 171.5, so it is an outlier.

questions.stem: Two netball teams, Team A and Team B, each played 15 games in a tournament. For each team, the number of goals scored in each game was recorded. The frequency table shows Team A’s data and the box plot shows Team B’s. Compare the distributions, supporting your answer by constructing a box plot for Team A.
questions.hint: Use the frequency table to write Team A’s 15 scores in order. Compare the medians for typical performance and IQR/range for spread.

parts.stem: Team A and Team B each played 15 games. Team A’s frequency table and Team B’s box plot are shown. Compare the distributions, constructing a box plot for Team A.
options: Team B has a slightly higher median; Team A has a smaller IQR and range, so Team A is more consistent
Team A has a higher median and a larger spread
Both teams have the same median and spread
Team A has a lower median and a larger spread
parts.hint: List Team A’s scores in order from the frequency table. Find its five-number summary and compare the medians and spreads with Team B.

steps.explain: Expand the frequency table into ordered scores: 19; 21; 22; 23; 24,24,24; 26,26,26,26; 27,27,27; 28.
For 15 scores, the median is the 8th value. Q1 is the 4th value of the lower seven and Q3 is the 4th value of the upper seven.
Team B’s plot gives 21,24,27,31,35. Its median 27 is slightly higher, while its IQR is 7 and range is 14; Team A’s IQR is 4 and range is 9.
steps.work: Team A is more consistent; Team B median is slightly higher

steps.explain: Conclusion: Team B scores slightly higher typically, while Team A’s results vary less.

questions.hint: Look at which side contains the long tail. Skew is named for the direction of the tail, not the location of the peak.

parts.stem: A set of data is displayed in this dot plot. Which description best fits the data?
parts.hint: Most values are near the right side of the plot. Identify the direction of the longer tail.

steps.explain: Most dots are clustered at the larger values, 9 and 10.
The tail stretches toward the smaller values on the left. A distribution with its tail to the left is negatively skewed.
Therefore the data are negatively skewed.

questions.stem: The graph displays the mean monthly rainfall in Sydney and Perth. Answer (i) and (ii).
questions.hint: Compare the paired bars for each month. Standard deviation describes the spread of the monthly rainfall values.

parts.stem: For how many months is the mean monthly rainfall higher in Perth than in Sydney?
parts.hint: Compare the Perth and Sydney bars month by month. Count months where the Perth bar is taller.

steps.explain: Scan the paired bars for each month. Perth’s bar is taller only in July.
No other month has Perth’s bar above Sydney’s.
Therefore the answer is one month.

parts.stem: For which city is the standard deviation of the mean monthly rainfall smaller? Justify without calculations.
options: Sydney, because its monthly rainfall varies less across the year
Perth, because its highest month is larger
Sydney, because it has a lower average
Perth, because most monthly values are below 50 mm
parts.hint: Standard deviation measures spread around the mean. Compare how widely each city’s monthly bars vary.

steps.explain: Sydney’s rainfall bars remain within a narrower vertical range over the year. Perth has very low months and a much higher peak.
A smaller spread indicates a smaller standard deviation.
Choose Sydney.

questions.hint: Use the cumulative frequencies to locate the middle 50%: find the scores at the first and third quartiles.

parts.stem: A cumulative frequency table for a data set is shown. What is the interquartile range?
parts.hint: There are 42 data values. Find the scores at the 25th and 75th percentiles using the cumulative frequencies.

steps.explain: The first quartile is around the 10.5th value. Cumulative frequency is 9 through score 2 and 16 through score 3, so Q1=3.
The third quartile is around the 31.5th value. Cumulative frequency is 20 through score 4 and 34 through score 5, so Q3=5.
Subtract to find the interquartile range.

questions.stem: A soccer referee wrote down the number of goals scored in 9 different games during the season: 2, 3, 3, 3, 5, 5, 8, 9, [omitted]. The last number has been omitted. The range is 10. What is the five-number summary for this data set?
questions.hint: Use the range to find the missing value first. Then use the ordered nine values to find the quartiles and median.

parts.stem: A soccer referee recorded the goals scored in 9 games: 2, 3, 3, 3, 5, 5, 8, 9, and one omitted value. The range is 10. What is the five-number summary?
parts.hint: The missing value must make the range 10. Then find the median and the medians of the lower and upper halves.

steps.explain: The current minimum is 2 and current maximum is 9. To make the range 10, the missing value must be 12.
The ordered list is 2,3,3,3,5,5,8,9,12. The fifth value is the median 5. The lower-half median is 3; the upper-half median is (8+9)/2=8.5.
Include the minimum and maximum.

questions.hint: Use the midpoint of each interval as its representative value. Find the weighted mean.

parts.stem: A grouped-data frequency table is shown. What is the mean for this set of data?
parts.hint: Use each class midpoint: 3, 8, 13 and 18. Multiply each midpoint by its frequency, then divide by total frequency.

steps.explain: Find each class midpoint: (1+5)/2=3, 8, 13 and 18.
Multiply by the class frequencies and add.
Divide by the total frequency, 3+6+8+9=26.

In Geography, 30 marks is the median. Half of Geography students scored above 30. This equals 28.

questions.stem: A small population consists of three students with heights 153 cm, 168 cm and 174 cm. Samples of varying sizes can be taken from this population. What is the mean of the mean heights of all the possible samples?
questions.hint: First calculate the population mean. The mean of the sampling distribution of the sample mean equals the population mean.

parts.stem: A small population consists of three students with heights 153 cm, 168 cm and 174 cm. Samples of varying sizes can be taken from this population. What is the mean of the mean heights of all possible samples?
parts.hint: The mean of the means of all possible samples equals the mean of the population.

steps.explain: Find the population mean by adding the three heights and dividing by 3.
For every sample size, the average of all possible sample means equals the population mean.
steps.work: Mean of all sample means = population mean

steps.explain: Therefore the required mean is 165 cm.

questions.stem: In a small business, the seven employees earn the following wages per week: $300, $490, $520, $590, $660, $680, $970. Answer (i) and (ii).
questions.hint: For (i), find the quartiles and compare the highest wage with the upper fence. For (ii), consider whether adding the same amount changes distances from the mean.

parts.stem: The weekly wages are $300, $490, $520, $590, $660, $680 and $970. Is $970 an outlier? Justify using the 1.5×IQR rule.
options: Yes, because $970 is above the upper fence $965
No, because the upper fence is $970
parts.hint: Find Q1 and Q3 from the ordered seven wages, then calculate the upper outlier fence.

steps.explain: The middle wage is $590. The lower and upper halves have medians $490 and $680.
Calculate the interquartile range and upper fence.
Since $970 is greater than $965, it is an outlier.

parts.stem: Each employee receives a $20 pay increase. What happens to the standard deviation of the wages?
parts.hint: Adding the same amount to every value shifts all data equally without changing their distances from the mean.

steps.explain: Adding $20 changes every wage by the same amount, so the mean also increases by $20.
Each distance from the mean remains unchanged: (wage+20)−(mean+20)=wage−mean.
steps.work: Deviation from new mean = original deviation

steps.explain: Standard deviation is based on these deviations, so it is unchanged.

questions.stem: Data from 200 recent house sales are grouped into class intervals and a cumulative frequency histogram is drawn. Answer (i) and (ii).
questions.hint: For (i), use cumulative frequency 100. For (ii), multiply each class centre by its frequency, add, then divide by the total number of sales.

parts.stem: Use the cumulative frequency graph to estimate the median house price.
parts.hint: There are 200 sales, so the median is read at cumulative frequency 100.

steps.explain: Half of 200 sales is 100. Locate cumulative frequency 100 on the vertical scale.
Read horizontally to the cumulative curve/graph, then down to the price axis. The estimate is about $393 000.
State the estimate in dollars.

parts.stem: Complete the class-centre frequency table and calculate the mean house price.
parts.hint: Use the four class centres 375, 385, 395 and 405 ($000), with frequencies 30, 50, 70 and 50.

steps.explain: Multiply each class centre by its frequency and add.
Add the frequencies.
Divide the weighted total by 200. The result is in thousands of dollars.

questions.stem: Twenty Year 12 students were surveyed. These students were asked how many hours of sport they play per week, to the nearest hour. The results are shown in the frequency table. What is the mean number of hours of sport played by the students per week?
questions.hint: Estimate each class by its midpoint, multiply by frequency, and divide the total by 20 students.

parts.stem: Twenty Year 12 students were surveyed about how many hours of sport they play each week. The frequency table is shown. What is the mean number of hours per week?
parts.hint: Use each interval midpoint (1, 4, 7, 10) as the representative number of hours.

steps.explain: Find the midpoint of each class interval.
steps.work: \(0	ext{–}2	o1;\quad3	ext{–}5	o4;\quad6	ext{–}8	o7;\quad9	ext{–}11	o10\)

steps.explain: Multiply each midpoint by the frequency and add.
Divide by the total frequency, 20.

questions.stem: The ages of members of a dance class are shown in the back-to-back stem-and-leaf plot. Pat claims that the women who attend the dance class are generally older than the men. Is Pat correct? Justify your answer by referring to the median and skewness of the two sets of data.
questions.hint: Read the ages from the stem-and-leaf plot, compare the medians, and describe the direction of each tail.

parts.stem: The back-to-back stem-and-leaf plot compares the ages of women and men in a dance class. Pat says the women are generally older than the men. Is Pat correct? Refer to the medians and skewness.
options: Yes; the women’s median age is 56.5, greater than the men’s 45; women are negatively skewed and men positively skewed
No; the men’s median age is greater
No; the women’s median is lower
parts.hint: Use the key to list the ages, find each median, then identify the direction of each distribution’s tail.

steps.explain: Read the leaves using the key. The women’s ordered ages are 32, 42, 44, 50, 54, 55, 58, 58, 63, 63, 64, 69.
There are 12 women, so their median is the average of the 6th and 7th values. Men’s ordered ages are 34,36,42,42,45,46,48,53,63, giving median 45.
The women’s data have a longer tail toward younger ages (negative skew), while the men’s data have a longer tail toward older ages (positive skew).
steps.work: Women: negative skew; men: positive skew

steps.explain: The women’s median is higher, so Pat’s claim is supported.

questions.stem: Terry and Kim each sat twenty class tests. Terry’s results are displayed in the box-and-whisker plot. Kim’s five-number summary is 67, 69, 71, 73, 75. Answer (i)–(iii).
questions.hint: Read Terry’s median and spread from the box plot. Use Kim’s five-number summary to compare typical score and variability.

parts.stem: Kim’s five-number summary is 67, 69, 71, 73, 75. Which set of values should be used to draw Kim’s box-and-whisker plot?
parts.hint: A five-number summary is listed in order: minimum, lower quartile, median, upper quartile, maximum.

steps.explain: Match each value to its place in the ordered five-number summary.
The whiskers go to the minimum 67 and maximum 75. The box runs from Q1=69 to Q3=73, with its median line at 71.
This is the first option.

parts.stem: What percentage of Terry’s test results were below 69?
parts.hint: Locate 69 on Terry’s box plot. It is the median.

steps.explain: The median line on Terry’s box plot is at 69.
Half the results lie below the median.
Therefore, 50% of Terry’s results were below 69.

parts.stem: Terry claims his results were better than Kim’s. Is he correct? Compare the summary statistics and skewness.
options: Yes; Terry has the higher maximum
No; Kim’s median is higher and Kim’s scores are more consistent
No; Terry’s range is smaller and his plot is symmetric
parts.hint: Compare the medians for typical performance, then compare the spreads and skewness shown by the box plots.

steps.explain: Terry’s median is 69. Kim’s median is 71, so Kim’s typical score is higher. At 69, 50% of Terry’s results but about 75% of Kim’s are above the mark.
Terry’s upper half and upper whisker are much longer than the lower side, so his scores are positively skewed. Kim’s five-number summary is balanced around 71, and her IQR and range are smaller.
steps.work: Terry: positive skew; Kim: more symmetric and less spread

steps.explain: Therefore Terry’s claim is not supported; Kim’s results were generally better and more consistent.

A graph displaying the data is to be included in a magazine article. The editor wishes to ensure that the graph is not misleading in any way. Which graph should the editor choose?
questions.hint: A fair column graph should start its vertical axis at zero so a small difference is not visually exaggerated.

parts.stem: A survey found that 48% preferred Brand X and 52% preferred Brand Y. The editor wants a column graph that is not misleading. Which graph should be used?
parts.hint: Choose a scale that starts at 0 so the small 4 percentage-point difference is not exaggerated.

steps.explain: The data differ by only four percentage points.
A vertical axis that starts at 46% makes the bars look very different even though the actual difference is small.
Graph B starts at 0 and shows the bars on a full percentage scale, so it represents the comparison fairly.

questions.stem: The July sale prices for properties in a suburb were $552 000, $595 000, $607 000, $607 000, $682 000 and $685 000. On 1 August, another property in the same suburb was sold for over one million dollars. If this property had been sold in July, what effect would it have had on the mean and median sale prices for July?
questions.hint: Place the very large value at the end of the ordered data. Check which middle value(s) determine the median and how the total changes.

parts.stem: The July sale prices for properties in a suburb were $552,000, $595,000, $607,000, $607,000, $682,000 and $685,000. A further property in the suburb sold for over $1,000,000. If it had been sold in July, what effect would it have had on the mean and median sale prices?
options: The mean changes and the median stays the same
Both the mean and median change
The mean stays the same and the median changes
Neither the mean nor the median changes
parts.hint: Insert the new high value into the ordered list. Compare the new middle value with the original median, and note its effect on the total.

steps.explain: The original six prices have middle values $607,000 and $607,000, so the median is $607,000.
A seventh price above $1,000,000 goes at the end. The fourth value is still $607,000, so the median is unchanged.
The new price is much larger than the previous prices, so it increases the total and therefore the mean.
Thus only the mean changes.
steps.work: \(\boxed{	ext{Mean changes; median stays the same}}\)

questions.stem: The mean of a set of ten scores is 14. Another two scores are included and the new mean is 16. What is the mean of the two additional scores?
questions.hint: Use mean × number of values to find each total. Subtract totals to isolate the two new scores.

parts.stem: The mean of a set of ten scores is 14. Another two scores are included and the new mean is 16. What is the mean of the two additional scores?
parts.hint: Find the total of the original 10 scores and the new 12 scores. Subtract to get the sum of the two added scores.

steps.explain: The original total is mean × number of scores.
The new total is 12 scores with mean 16.
The two new scores total 192−140=52. Divide by 2 to find their mean.

questions.stem: Christina has completed three Mathematics tests. Her mean mark is 72%. What mark (out of 100) does she have to get in her next test to increase her mean mark to 73%?
questions.hint: Calculate the total marks needed after four tests and subtract the marks she already has.

parts.stem: Christina has completed three Mathematics tests. Her mean mark is 72%. What mark out of 100 does she need in her next test to increase her mean mark to 73%?
parts.hint: Work out the total marks for three tests at 72%, then find the four-test total needed for a 73% mean.

steps.explain: Her first three tests total 3×72=216 marks.
A mean of 73 after four tests requires a total of 4×73=292 marks.
Subtract the current total from the target total to find the required fourth mark.

questions.stem: This set of data is arranged in order from smallest to largest: 5, 6, 11, x, 13, 18, 25. The range is six less than twice the value of x. Which one of the following is true?
questions.hint: First form an equation from the range. Once x is known, read the median and quartiles from the ordered list.

parts.stem: This set of data is arranged in order from smallest to largest: 5, 6, 11, x, 13, 18, 25. The range is six less than twice the value of x. Which statement is true?
options: The median is 12 and the interquartile range is 7
The median is 12 and the interquartile range is 12
The median is 13 and the interquartile range is 7
The median is 13 and the interquartile range is 12
parts.hint: Use the range equation to find x. Then read the median and quartiles from the ordered seven values.

steps.explain: The range is maximum minus minimum: 25−5=20. It is six less than twice x, so 20=2x−6.
Solve for x.
The ordered values are 5,6,11,13,13,18,25. The median is the 4th value, 13. Q1 is 6 and Q3 is 18.
Subtract quartiles to find IQR.

questions.stem: Jason travels to work by car on all five days of his working week, leaving home at 7 am each day. He compares his travel times using roads without tolls and roads with tolls over a period of 12 working weeks. He records his travel times (in minutes) in the back-to-back stem-and-leaf plot. Answer (i)–(iii).
questions.hint: Use the stem as the tens digit and the leaves as ones. Compare middle values for the median and overall spread/tails for the distributions.

parts.stem: What is the modal travel time when Jason uses roads without tolls?
parts.hint: Find the stem-and-leaf value that appears most often on the “Without tolls” side.

steps.explain: The mode is the value that occurs most often. Use the stem as the tens and the leaf as the ones.
The leaf 2 appears four times in the stem 5 row, more often than any other travel time.
So the modal travel time is 52 minutes.

parts.stem: What is the median travel time when Jason uses roads without tolls?
parts.hint: There are 30 values on the “Without tolls” side. Average the 15th and 16th ordered values.

steps.explain: There are 30 travel times. For an even number of values, the median is the mean of the two middle values.
Reading the ordered data gives 50 and 51 minutes in those positions.
Calculate their average.

parts.stem: How do the two travel-time distributions compare in spread and skewness?
options: Without tolls has much greater spread and is fairly symmetric; with tolls has smaller spread and is positively skewed
Without tolls is positively skewed and has smaller spread
With tolls has greater spread and is negatively skewed
Both have equal spread and are symmetric
parts.hint: Compare the ranges and look for the direction of the longer tail in each distribution.

steps.explain: The no-toll times run from 39 to 61 minutes, while toll-road times run from 35 to 90 minutes.
steps.work: No tolls range \(=61-39=22\); with tolls range \(=90-35=55\)

steps.explain: The no-toll values cluster fairly evenly around the middle. The toll-road values cluster at the lower end with a tail toward longer times.
steps.work: No tolls: fairly symmetric; with tolls: right tail

steps.explain: Thus no-toll times have the smaller spread; toll-road times are more spread and positively skewed.
steps.work: \(\boxed{	ext{No tolls: smaller spread, roughly symmetric; tolls: larger spread, positive skew}}\)

questions.stem: A retailer has collected data on the number of televisions that he sold each week in 2012. He grouped the data into classes and displayed the data using a cumulative frequency histogram and polygon (ogive). Answer (i) and (ii).
questions.hint: For the quartiles, use cumulative frequencies 13 and 39 out of 52 weeks. Remember a grouped class gives an interval, not an exact weekly sales value.

parts.stem: Use the cumulative frequency polygon to determine the interquartile range of weekly television sales.
parts.hint: The maximum cumulative frequency is 52. Find Q1 at cumulative frequency 13 and Q3 at 39.

steps.explain: There are 52 weeks. The lower quartile is at 52÷4=13 and the upper quartile at 3×13=39.
Read from the graph: Q1 is about 190 televisions and Q3 about 470 televisions.
Subtract the quartiles.

parts.stem: Oscar says the retailer sold exactly 300 televisions in 6 weeks. Is he correct?
options: Yes, the graph gives exactly 300 for six weeks
No; grouped data only show that sales were between 250 and 350 in 6 weeks
No; sales were between 350 and 450 in 6 weeks
parts.hint: The graph groups sales into intervals. Use the rise in cumulative frequency around the 300 class centre.

steps.explain: The cumulative frequency rises from about 22 to 28 across the class centred at 300.
That class represents weekly sales between 250 and 350, not exactly 300.
So it is not possible to say they sold exactly 300 in each of 6 weeks.

questions.stem: The test results in English and Mathematics for a class were recorded and displayed in the box-and-whisker plots. Answer (i) and (ii).
questions.hint: Use the box edges for quartiles, the centre line for median, and whisker ends for extremes. Compare spread and tail direction.

parts.stem: What is the interquartile range for English?
parts.hint: Read the lower and upper edges of the English box; these are Q1 and Q3.

steps.explain: From the English box plot, the lower quartile is 50 and the upper quartile is 80.
The interquartile range is Q3 minus Q1.
Therefore the English IQR is 30 marks.

parts.stem: Which comparison of the English and Mathematics distributions is correct?
options: Both are negatively skewed; English has a wider spread and a higher maximum, while Mathematics has a higher median
Both are positively skewed and have the same spread
English has a higher median and smaller spread
Mathematics has a lower median and wider spread
parts.hint: Compare medians, quartile ranges, ranges and the balance of each box plot.

steps.explain: Both plots have longer lower sides/whiskers, indicating negative skew. English has Q1=50,Q3=80, so IQR=30; Mathematics has Q1=65,Q3=80, so IQR=15.
steps.work: Both negatively skewed; English IQR 30, Mathematics IQR 15

steps.explain: English range is 95−10=85; Mathematics range is 90−50=40. English maximum is higher, while Mathematics median 75 exceeds English median 70.
Therefore English scores are more spread and have a higher maximum, but Mathematics has the higher median.

questions.stem: A data set of nine scores has a median of 7. The scores 6, 6, 12 and 17 are added to this data set. What is the median of the data set now?
questions.hint: The original middle score is 7. Check how many new scores go below 7 and how many go above 7.

parts.stem: A data set of nine scores has a median of 7. The scores 6, 6, 12 and 17 are added to this data set. What is the median of the data set now?
parts.hint: The original median is 7. Count how many added values fall below and above 7.

steps.explain: With nine scores, the original 5th score is 7.
Two new scores, 6 and 6, are below 7; two new scores, 12 and 17, are above 7. The middle position remains at the original middle value.
steps.work: Two added below, two added above

steps.explain: So the median does not change.

questions.stem: The marks for a Science test and a Mathematics test are presented in box-and-whisker plots. Which measure must be the same for both tests?
questions.hint: A box extends from the lower quartile to the upper quartile. Its length represents the interquartile range.

parts.stem: The box-and-whisker plots show the marks for a Science test and a Mathematics test. Which measure must be the same for both tests?
parts.hint: The interquartile range is the width of the box. Compare the two box widths.

steps.explain: In a box plot, the left and right edges of the box are Q1 and Q3.
The two boxes have equal widths, so their Q3−Q1 values are equal.
steps.work: Science box width = Mathematics box width

steps.explain: Therefore the interquartile ranges must be equal.

questions.hint: Use row and column totals to check the shaded entry. The correct female part-time count is the female total minus female full-time count.

parts.stem: Leanne copied a two-way table into her book. One value in the shaded section is incorrect. Which value has been incorrectly copied?
options: The number of males in full-time work
The number of males in part-time work
The number of females in full-time work
The number of females in part-time work
parts.hint: Check whether the row and column totals agree with the entries. Find the shaded cell that makes a total inconsistent.

steps.explain: Check the full-time row: 279+356=635, so these entries agree.
Check the male column: 279+187=466, also correct. The female part-time entry should equal 885−356=529.
The table lists 439 in that cell, so this is the copied value that is wrong.

questions.stem: Consider the following set of scores: 3, 5, 5, 6, 8, 8, 9, 10, 10, 50. Answer (i) and (ii).
questions.hint: Calculate the mean from the total and count. For the median, use the middle value(s) in the ordered scores.

parts.stem: The scores are 3, 5, 5, 6, 8, 8, 9, 10, 10 and 50. Calculate the mean.
parts.hint: Add all ten scores and divide the total by 10.

steps.explain: Add the scores, keeping repeated values.
There are 10 scores.
Divide total by count.

parts.stem: What is the effect on the mean and median of removing the outlier 50?
options: The mean decreases; the median stays 8
The mean stays the same; the median changes
Both the mean and median decrease
The mean decreases; the median increases
parts.hint: Recalculate the total and count without 50. The median is the average of the two middle values for ten values.

steps.explain: Without 50, the sum is 114−50=64 and there are 9 values.
The middle value among the remaining nine scores is 8. The original median was the average of the 5th and 6th values, also 8.
Thus the mean falls substantially while the median remains unchanged.

questions.stem: A set of data is represented by the cumulative frequency histogram and ogive. What is the best approximation for the interquartile range for this set of data?
questions.hint: Find the scores at cumulative frequencies 200 and 600 for a total of 800 values.

parts.stem: A set of data is represented by a cumulative frequency histogram and ogive. What is the best approximation for the interquartile range?
parts.hint: There are 800 values. Read Q1 at cumulative frequency 200 and Q3 at 600, then subtract.

steps.explain: Find the quartile cumulative frequencies.
Read the graph: the lower quartile is about 45 and the upper quartile about 80.
Subtract.

questions.hint: Use the quartile positions: about 75% of values lie below the upper quartile.

parts.stem: Two groups of people were surveyed about their weekly wages. Which statement is true?
options: The same percentage in each group earned more than $325 per week
Approximately 75% of people under 21 earned less than $350 per week
Approximately 75% of people aged 21 and older earned more than $350 per week
Approximately 50% of people in each group earned between $325 and $350 per week
parts.hint: Read $350 on the plots. For the under-21 group, it is about the upper quartile, so about 75% of that group is below it.

steps.explain: Locate $350 on the horizontal scale and compare it with the quartiles for the under-21 box plot.
By definition, about 75% of observations lie below the upper quartile.
steps.work: \(75\%\) of under-21 wages are below about $350

steps.explain: This matches statement B.

questions.hint: A cumulative frequency counts students who watched that many movies or fewer. Subtract CF(3) from CF(4).

parts.stem: Students were surveyed about how many movies they had watched in the last week. The results are shown in this cumulative frequency histogram. How many students said they watched four movies last week?
parts.hint: Read the cumulative frequency at 3 movies and at 4 movies. The number who watched exactly 4 is the difference.

steps.explain: The cumulative frequency through 3 movies is 25 students.
The cumulative frequency through 4 movies is 35 students.
Subtract to find the number who watched exactly 4.

questions.stem: Barry constructed a back-to-back stem-and-leaf plot to compare the ages of students attending Barry's Ballroom Dancing Studio.
questions.hint: Use the key to read ages. Count leaves, compare tails, and remember grouped-data means use class centres.

parts.stem: Write a brief statement that compares the distribution of the ages of males and females from this set of data.
options: There are more males; male ages are positively skewed and female ages negatively skewed
There are more females; both are positively skewed
There are equal numbers; both are symmetric
There are more males; both are negatively skewed
parts.hint: Count the leaves on each side, then look for the longer tail in each distribution.

steps.explain: Count the leaves: there are more leaves on the male side. The male values extend toward older ages, with a longer high-age tail.
steps.work: More males; male tail toward older ages

steps.explain: Female ages extend farther toward the younger end, giving a negative skew. Male ages have positive skew.
steps.work: Females: negative skew; males: positive skew

steps.explain: This matches the first statement.

keyPoints.text: distribution of the ages of males and females
keyPoints.note: Compare the two sides of the plot.

parts.stem: What is the mode of this set of data?
parts.hint: Combine both sides and find the age that occurs most often.

steps.explain: Use each stem as the tens digit and each leaf as the ones digit. The age 64 appears twice among males and twice among females.
No other age appears as often in the combined data.
Therefore the mode is 64 years.

keyPoints.text: mode of this set of data
keyPoints.note: Find the value that occurs most often.

parts.stem: Liam decided to use a grouped frequency distribution table to calculate the mean age of the students at Barry’s Ballroom Dancing Studio. For the age group 30–39 years, what is the value of the product of the class centre and the frequency?
parts.hint: Find the midpoint of 30–39 and count all ages in the 30s.

steps.explain: The class centre is the midpoint of the class limits.
There are five students aged 30–39 in total.
Multiply centre by frequency.

keyPoints.note: Use the class midpoint and count leaves in that interval.

parts.stem: Liam correctly calculated the mean from the grouped frequency distribution table to be 39.5. What is the reason for the difference in the two answers?
options: Grouped data uses class centres as approximations; the original ages give an exact mean
The grouped mean always includes an outlier
The original ages are rounded to class centres
A grouped mean is always smaller
parts.hint: A grouped frequency table replaces all values in a class by one representative value.

steps.explain: The original mean uses each student’s exact age.
steps.work: Raw data: each age is used

steps.explain: For grouped data, every age in a class is represented by that class centre. This is an approximation.
Therefore the grouped mean can differ from the exact mean based on the original ages.
steps.work: \(\boxed{	ext{Class centres make the grouped mean approximate}}\)

keyPoints.text: mean from the grouped frequency distribution table

questions.stem: A census was conducted of the 33 171 households in Sunnytown. Each household was asked to indicate the number of cars registered to that household. The results are summarised in the following table.
questions.hint: Read frequencies for the mode, use cars × households for total stickers, and multiply the no-car fraction by 360° for its sector angle. Use the step graph for parking cost.

parts.stem: Determine the mode number of cars in a household.
parts.hint: The mode is the number of cars with the greatest frequency.

steps.explain: Compare the frequencies in the table. The largest count is 13,918.
That frequency corresponds to households with 2 cars.
So the mode is 2 cars.

keyPoints.text: mode number of cars in a household
keyPoints.note: The mode is the category with the greatest frequency.

parts.stem: Explain what is meant by the mode number of cars in a household.
options: The number of cars with the greatest frequency registered per household; in this survey, the greatest number of households had 2 cars
The number of cars that is the average for all households
The number of cars held by half of all households
The largest number of cars registered by any household
parts.hint: The mode is the value that occurs most often.

steps.explain: The mode is the category with the greatest frequency.
The table shows 2 cars has the greatest number of households.
So most households surveyed had 2 cars.

keyPoints.text: mode number of cars in a household
keyPoints.note: In words, describe what the most frequent car count tells you.

parts.stem: Sunnytown Council issued a “free parking” sticker for each car registered to a household in Sunnytown. How many parking stickers were issued?
parts.hint: Multiply each car count by its frequency and add the products.

steps.explain: Households with 0 cars receive no stickers. Count the cars in the other groups.
Calculate each product and add.
That is the number of registered cars and stickers.

keyPoints.text: each car registered to a household
keyPoints.note: Multiply each car count by its frequency, then add.

parts.stem: The council represented the results of the census in a sector graph. What is the angle in the sector representing the households with no cars? Give your answer to the nearest degree.
parts.hint: The angle is the no-car proportion of the total, multiplied by 360°.

steps.explain: There are 2,735 households with no cars out of 33,171 total.
Multiply the fraction by a full circle.
Round to the nearest degree.

keyPoints.note: Use this group’s share of the total to find a fraction of 360°.

The step graph shows a cost of $10 throughout that interval.
Therefore the visitor pays $10.

questions.stem: Jo is researching the relationship between the ages of teenage characters in television series and the ages of actors playing these characters. After collecting the data, Jo finds that the correlation coefficient is \(0.4564\). A scatterplot showing the data is drawn. The line of best fit with equation \(y=-7.51+1.85x\), is also drawn. Describe and interpret the data and other information provided, with reference to the context given.
options: The data show a moderate positive association. As character age rises, actor age tends to rise; the fitted line suggests about 1.85 extra actor-years for each extra character-year.
The data show a strong negative association. Older characters are generally played by younger actors, and actor age falls by 1.85 years per year.
There is no linear association because the correlation is close to zero; the line means actor age stays constant.
The data show a perfect positive association, so every actor is exactly 1.85 years older than the character.
questions.hint: Use the sign and size of r to describe the pattern, then interpret the slope of the fitted line in this story.

steps.explain: The correlation coefficient is positive, so the overall pattern goes upward. Since 0.4564 is not close to 1, the linear association is moderate rather than very strong.

questions.stem: For a sample of 17 inland towns in Australia, the height above sea level, \(x\) (metres), and the average maximum daily temperature, \(y\) (°C), were recorded. The graph shows the data as well as a regression line. The equation of the regression line is \(y=29.2-0.011x\). The correlation coefficient is \(r=-0.494\). The graph below shows the relationship between the latitude, \(x\) (degrees south), and the average maximum daily temperature, \(y\) (°C), for the same 17 towns, as well as a regression line. The equation of the regression line is \(y=45.6-0.683x\). The correlation coefficient is \(r=-0.897\). Another inland town in Australia is 540 m above sea level. Its latitude is 28 degrees south.
questions.hint: For the prediction, substitute the given height into the regression equation. For the gradient, keep the units and direction in mind. For the second prediction question, compare |r| values.

parts.stem: By using the equation of the regression line, predict the average maximum daily temperature, in degrees Celsius, for a town that is 540 m above sea level. Give your answer correct to one decimal place.

parts.stem: The gradient of the regression line is −0.011. Interpret the value of this gradient in the given context.
options: For every 1 m increase in height, predicted average maximum temperature decreases by 0.011°C
For every 1°C increase in temperature, height decreases by 0.011 m
For every 100 m increase in height, temperature increases by 0.011°C
parts.hint: The gradient tells how much the predicted temperature changes when height increases by 1 metre.

steps.explain: In the equation, x is height in metres and y is temperature in degrees Celsius. The gradient is the change in y for each 1-unit increase in x.

parts.stem: Which measurement, height above sea level or latitude, would be better to use to predict this town’s average maximum daily temperature? Give a reason for your answer.
options: Height, because its correlation coefficient has the larger absolute value
Height, because its correlation is negative
Latitude, because |−0.897| is greater than |−0.494|, so its linear association is stronger
Latitude, because a negative correlation proves latitude causes temperature to change
parts.hint: Compare the absolute sizes of the two correlation coefficients. The value closer to 1 in magnitude shows a stronger linear association.

steps.explain: The height correlation is −0.494 and the latitude correlation is −0.897. Both are negative, so both trends decrease.

questions.stem: A cricket is an insect. The male cricket produces a chirping sound. A scientist wants to explore the relationship between temperature in degrees Celsius and the number of cricket chirps heard in a 15-second time interval. Once a day for 20 days, the scientist collects data. Based on the 20 data points, the scientist provides the information below. A box-plot of the temperature data is shown. The mean temperature in the dataset is 0.525°C below the median temperature in the dataset. A total of 684 chirps was counted when collecting the 20 data points. The scientist fits a least-squares regression line using the data, where x is the temperature in degrees Celsius and y is the number of chirps heard in a 15-second time interval. The equation of this line is \(y=-10.6063+bx\), where b is the slope of the regression line. The least-squares regression line passes through the point \((\bar{x},\bar{y})\). Calculate the number of chirps expected when the temperature is 19 °C. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.
questions.hint: Read the median from the box plot. Use it to find the mean temperature, then use both sample means to find b before substituting 19°C.

parts.stem: At the start of 2020, Jim decides to buy the truck that has travelled 55 000 kilometres. The value of the truck decreases by 25% each year. During which year will the truck be valued at less than $5000?
parts.hint: A 25% decrease leaves 75% of the previous year’s value. Use $31,670 as the starting value, then find when it drops below $5,000.

steps.explain: A 25% yearly decrease means the value is multiplied by 75%, or 0.75, each year. Start with the predicted purchase price.
Find when the value reaches $5,000.

The truck must be held for more than 6.4166 years to be below $5,000. Check the surrounding whole years: after 6 years it is still above $5,000, and after 7 it is below. Starting at the beginning of 2020, the threshold is crossed during 2026.

questions.stem: The four scatterplots below show different data sets. Which of the data sets has the largest positive correlation coefficient?
questions.hint: A positive correlation rises from left to right. Among the rising plots, the largest \(r\) belongs to the one whose points lie closest to a straight line.

steps.explain: Check the direction of each scatterplot first. Plot A is flat (about zero correlation). Plots C and D both slope downward from left to right, so their correlation is negative. Only plot B rises from left to right.
steps.work:
A: no trend, \(r \approx 0\).
B: rises, \(r > 0\).
C: falls, \(r < 0\).
D: falls, \(r < 0\).

steps.explain: B is the only plot with a positive direction, and its points lie almost exactly on an upward straight line (dashed), so \(r\) is very close to \(+1\). A negative \(r\), even a strong one like C, is always smaller than any positive \(r\).

parts.stem: Determine the gradient of the line of best fit shown on the graph.
parts.hint: Choose two clear points on the purple best-fit line, for example (11,146) and (15,170). Gradient is vertical change divided by horizontal change.

steps.explain: The horizontal coordinate is age a in years and the vertical coordinate is height h in centimetres. Use the two highlighted points on the fitted line.

options: The line predicts an average height increase of about 6 cm for each additional year of age.
Each male grows exactly 6 cm every year.
The average age increases by 6 years for each centimetre.
The tallest male is 6 cm taller than the shortest.
parts.hint: Attach units to the gradient: vertical units are centimetres and horizontal units are years.

steps.explain: The gradient 6 is calculated as 6 centimetres of height change for every 1 year of age change.

questions.stem: Which of the following relationships would most likely show a negative correlation?
options: The population of a town and the number of hospitals in that town.
The hours spent training for a race and the time taken to complete the race.
The price per litre of petrol and the number of people riding bicycles to work.
The number of pets per household and the number of computers per household.
questions.hint: Negative correlation means one variable tends to go down as the other goes up. Think about how more training affects race completion time.

steps.explain: For negative correlation, increases in one variable are associated with decreases in the other.
steps.work: Check which option has a clear reason for one quantity to decrease when the other increases.

steps.explain: As training hours increase, the time needed to finish the race tends to decrease. This is a negative association.
steps.work: \(\boxed{\text{Hours spent training and time taken to complete the race}}\)

keyPoints.note: One variable tends to decrease while the other increases.

questions.stem: Tourists visit a park where steam erupts from a particular geyser. The brochure for the park has a graph of the data collected for this geyser over a period of time. The graph shows the duration of an eruption and the time until the next eruption, timed from the end of one eruption to the beginning of the next.
questions.hint: Use the horizontal axis for duration and the vertical axis for waiting time. Convert one hour to 60 minutes before reading the second answer.

parts.stem: Tony sees an eruption that lasts 4 minutes. Based on the data in the graph, what is the minimum time that he can expect to wait for the next eruption?
parts.hint: At duration 4 minutes, look at the plotted points with x=4 and select the smallest wait time.

steps.explain: The horizontal axis gives eruption duration. Locate 4 minutes and move vertically through the points at that duration.

questions.stem:
A continuous random variable \(X\) has a probability density function defined by:

\(f(x) = \begin{cases} ax(10-x) & 0 \leq x \leq 10 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\)

If the total probability is normalized, which of the following expressions correctly verifies the value of \(a\)?
questions.hint: For a valid PDF, $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\,dx = 1$. Integrate $ax(10-x)$ over $[0, 10]$ and set equal to 1.
questions.solution:
$\displaystyle\int_0^{10} ax(10-x)\,dx = 1$.

$a\displaystyle\int_0^{10}(10x - x^2)\,dx = a\left[5x^2 - \frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^{10} = a\left(500 - \frac{1000}{3}\right) = a \cdot \frac{500}{3} = 1$.

$\therefore a = \dfrac{3}{500}$ ✓

steps.explain: We begin by setting up the integral equation for a normalized probability density function. The total probability over the domain of the random variable must equal one, which is expressed as the definite integral of the function from zero to ten.
Next, we factor out the constant parameter and find the antiderivative of the quadratic polynomial term by term using standard power integration rules.

We substitute the limits of integration into the antiderivative to find the definite value. Subtracting the lower limit of zero from the evaluated upper limit of ten gives the simplified coefficient equation.
Finally, we solve the algebraic equation for the parameter by taking the reciprocal of the fraction on the left side, which establishes the correct verified value.

questions.stem: Using the probability density function \(f(x) = \dfrac{3}{500}x(10-x)\) for \(0 \leq x \leq 10\), find the cumulative distribution function \(F(x)\) within this domain.
questions.hint: $F(x) = \int_0^x f(t)\,dt$. Integrate $\frac{3}{500}t(10-t)$ from 0 to $x$.

steps.explain: We begin by defining the relationship between a cumulative distribution function and a probability density function. The cumulative distribution function is obtained by integrating the probability density function from the lower limit of its support up to a variable point.
Next, we factor the constant coefficient out of the integral and expand the polynomial inside the integrand to simplify the application of integration rules.
We perform the integration by applying the power rule to each term of the polynomial, finding the antiderivative and preparing it to be evaluated at the boundary limits.
We substitute the variable limit into the antiderivative expression, simplify the constants by distributing the coefficient, and factor the expression to find the final algebraic form.

questions.stem: Using the cumulative distribution function \(F(x) = \dfrac{x^2(15-x)}{500}\) for \(0 \leq x \leq 10\), find the probability that a randomly selected wait time is more than 7 minutes.

steps.explain: We begin by setting up the equation for the probability of an event exceeding a certain value. Using the complement rule, the probability that the random variable is greater than seven is equal to one minus the probability that it is less than or equal to seven, which is represented by the cumulative distribution function evaluated at seven.
Next, we substitute the value of seven into the expression for the cumulative distribution function to compute the accumulated probability up to that point.
We simplify the numerical expression. We square seven, subtract seven from fifteen, and multiply the resulting values in the numerator before dividing by the denominator.

Finally, we subtract the evaluated cumulative probability from one to find the final complement probability. A common mistake here is subtracting incorrectly from one, so we double-check the subtraction to ensure decimal accuracy.

questions.stem: The length of time, in minutes, that a customer queues to buy toilet paper is a continuous random variable \(X\) with probability density function \(f(x) = k(64-x^2)\) for \(0 \le x \le 8\), and \(f(x)=0\) otherwise, where \(k\) is a constant.

parts.stem: (a) What is the value of the constant \(k\) that makes \(f(x)\) a valid probability density function?
parts.hint: The total area under a probability density function must equal 1 — integrate \(f(x)\) over its domain \(0\le x\le8\) (not a symmetric range) and set the result equal to 1.

steps.explain: The total area under a probability density function must equal 1, so integrate \(f(x)\) over its domain and set the result to 1.
Find the primitive and evaluate between the limits.
Set this equal to 1 and solve for \(k\).

Option B comes from mistakenly integrating over a symmetric domain \([-8,8]\) instead of the actual domain \([0,8]\) (doubling the integral). Option C comes from flipping the equation the wrong way (writing \(k=\tfrac{1024}{3}\) instead of its reciprocal). Option D comes from dropping the "3" in the final simplification.
steps.work: Compare: symmetric-domain slip \(\to\tfrac{3}{2048}\); flipped reciprocal \(\to\tfrac{1024}{3}\); dropped numerator \(\to\tfrac{1}{1024}\)

parts.stem: (b) Find the cumulative distribution function \(F(x)\) for \(0 \le x \le 8\).
parts.hint: \(F(x) = \displaystyle\int_0^x f(t)\,dt\). Integrate \(k(64-t^2)\) from \(0\) to \(x\).

steps.explain: Integrate the pdf from \(0\) to \(x\), using \(k=\tfrac{3}{1024}\).
Evaluate at the upper limit \(x\) (the lower limit gives 0).
Distribute the \(\tfrac{3}{1024}\) across both terms and simplify.

parts.stem: (c) Find the probability that a customer queues for longer than 5 minutes, correct to 4 significant figures.
parts.hint: \(P(X>5) = 1 - F(5)\), using the CDF found in part (b).

steps.explain: Use the complement rule with the CDF from part (b).
Evaluate \(F(5)\).
Complete the subtraction and round to 4 significant figures.

questions.stem: Find the median of the continuous probability distribution defined by \( f(x)=\dfrac{x^3}{64} \) on \( [0,4] \).

steps.explain: The median \( m \) of a continuous distribution satisfies \( \displaystyle\int_0^m f(x)\,dx = \dfrac12 \).
Integrate, then evaluate between the limits 0 and \( m \).
Multiply both sides by 256 to isolate \( m^4 \).
Take the fourth root of both sides. Since \( 128=16\times8 \) and \( \sqrt[4]{16}=2 \), simplify the surd.

questions.stem: A continuous random variable has probability density function \( f(x) = \begin{cases} ax^2, & 0\le x\le6 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \)

parts.stem: (a) Find the value of \( a \).

steps.explain: Every probability density function must integrate to 1 over its domain — this reflects total probability.
Integrate, factoring the constant \( a \) out.
Evaluate the bracket at the limits.
Solve for \( a \).

parts.stem: (b) Using \( a=\dfrac{1}{72} \), find \( P(3\le X\le5) \).

steps.explain: The probability over an interval is the definite integral of \( f(x) \) across that interval.
Integrate, then evaluate between the limits 3 and 5.
Evaluate the cubes and subtract.
Simplify the resulting fraction to lowest terms.
Part (a): for \(f(x)=ax^2\) to be a valid probability density function on \([0,6]\), the total area under the curve must equal 1.
Integrate and substitute the limits.
Solve for \(a\).
Part (b): find \(P(3 \le X \le 5)\) by integrating the pdf \(f(x) = \dfrac{x^2}{72}\) between \(x=3\) and \(x=5\).
Substitute the limits and simplify to a single fraction, then a decimal approximation.

questions.stem: The probability density function for the continuous random variable \(X\) is given by \(f(x)=|1-x|\) for \(0 \le x \le 2\), and \(f(x)=0\) otherwise.

parts.stem: (a) Find \(P(X \le 1.5)\).
parts.hint: The function \(y=|1-x|\) forms two straight-line pieces on \([0,1]\) and \([1,2]\) — the shaded area under it is made of two triangles. Use \(\text{Area}=\tfrac12\times\text{base}\times\text{height}\) for each.

steps.explain: Recognise the pdf as two straight lines meeting at \((1,0)\): a triangle of base 1, height 1 over \([0,1]\), and a smaller triangle of base 0.5, height 0.5 over \([1,1.5]\) — both regions lie below \(x=1.5\).
steps.work: Region: full triangle on \([0,1]\) + partial triangle on \([1,1.5]\)

steps.explain: Compute the area of each triangle using \(\tfrac12\times\text{base}\times\text{height}\), then add.
Add the two areas.

parts.stem: (b) Find \(P(1 \le X \le 2)\).
parts.hint: This is a single right-angled triangle from \(x=1\) to \(x=2\), with base 1 and height \(f(2)=1\).

steps.explain: The region from \(x=1\) to \(x=2\) is a single triangle with base 1 (from \(x=1\) to \(x=2\)) and height 1 (since \(f(2)=|1-2|=1\)).
Apply the triangle area formula.

questions.stem: Which of the following graphs could NOT represent a probability density function \(f(x)\)?
options: A cubic-like curve, rising and entirely above the \(x\)-axis
An upward parabola that dips below the \(x\)-axis before rising
An upward parabola, entirely above the \(x\)-axis
A straight line, rising and entirely above the \(x\)-axis
questions.hint: A probability density function must satisfy \(f(x) \ge 0\) everywhere in its domain — it can never dip below the \(x\)-axis.

steps.explain: A key requirement of any probability density function is that it can never be negative, since a "negative probability density" is meaningless.
steps.work: Requirement: \(f(x) \ge 0\) for all \(x\) in the domain

steps.explain: Three of the graphs (upward parabola entirely above the axis, rising cubic-like curve above the axis, rising straight line above the axis) satisfy \(f(x)\ge0\) throughout. Only the parabola that dips below the \(x\)-axis takes negative values over part of its domain.
steps.work: The dipping parabola has \(f(x)<0\) for some \(x\)

steps.explain: This violates the non-negativity requirement, so it could NOT represent a valid pdf.
steps.work: \(\therefore\) the parabola dipping below the \(x\)-axis is NOT a valid pdf

questions.stem: Let \(X\) be a continuous random variable whose probability density function is \(f(x)=\frac{3}{4}(2x-x^2)\) for \(0\le x\le2\). What is the mode of \(X\)?
questions.hint: The mode is where the density reaches its maximum. Differentiate the density and check the interval.

keyPoints.text: Let \(X\) be a continuous random variable whose probability density function is \(f(x)=\frac{3}{4}(2x-x^2)\)

steps.explain: Differentiate the density on \(0\le x\le 2\).

parts.stem: (a) What value of \(k\) makes the given function a probability density?

steps.explain: A valid probability density function must integrate to 1 over its full domain.
Find the antiderivative and evaluate at the bounds.
Simplify the bracketed expression. Pitfall: sign errors when expanding the negative of the lower-bound evaluation are the most common mistake here.

parts.hint: Set the integral of the density over its support equal to 1.

keyPoints.note: Set the total area under the density on its support equal to 1.

parts.stem: (b) Fully define the cumulative distribution function \( F(x) \).

steps.explain: For \( x\lt 1 \), no probability has accumulated yet; for \( x\gt 4 \), all of it has.
For \( 1\le x\le4 \), integrate the density from 1 to x.

Evaluate and simplify, substituting the lower bound value \( \tfrac13-1+2=\tfrac43 \). Pitfall: forgetting to subtract the constant of integration (the lower-bound value) leaves the "-1/9" term off, giving the third distractor.
Combine all three intervals to state the full piecewise cumulative distribution function.

parts.hint: Integrate the density from the lower support endpoint and add the two outer pieces.

keyPoints.note: Integrate the density from the lower support endpoint and add the two outer pieces.

parts.stem: (c) Which interval is confirmed to contain the median of \(X\)?

steps.explain: The median m is the value satisfying \( F(m)=0.5 \). Evaluate \( F \) at both boundary values using the formula from part (b).
Compute this numerically.
Repeat for \( x=3.3 \).

Since \( F(3.2)\lt 0.5 \) and \( F(3.3)\gt 0.5 \), and \( F \) is continuous and increasing, the median must lie between them. Pitfall: this argument only works because F is monotonic increasing on this interval — always confirm that first.

parts.hint: Evaluate F at both endpoints and compare each value with 0.5.

keyPoints.note: The median is where the cumulative probability crosses 0.5; compare F at the endpoints.

parts.solution: Since \(F(3.2)\approx0.479<0.5\) and \(F(3.3)\approx0.5296>0.5\), the median lies in \((3.2,3.3)\).

questions.stem: A continuous random variable, \(X\), has a probability density function given by \(f(x)=\begin{cases}\frac{k}{2x-1} & 1\le x\le4 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}\)

keyPoints.text: Show that the value of \(k\) is \(\frac{2}{\ln 7}\).
keyPoints.note: Identify the given information in this exact phrase first, then connect it to the rule or calculation shown in the solution.

steps.explain: Set the total probability over the support equal to 1.
Integrate using the reverse chain rule.
Solve for k.

parts.stem: Find \(P(X<2)\).
parts.hint: Integrate the density from its lower support bound 1 to 2, then substitute k.

keyPoints.note: Identify the given information in this exact phrase first, then connect it to the rule or calculation shown in the solution.

steps.explain: Write the probability as the area under the density from 1 to 2.
Evaluate the logarithmic integral.
Substitute k=2/ln 7.

questions.stem: Let \(X\) be a continuous random variable whose probability density function is \(f(x)=\frac{3x^2}{8}\) for \(0<x<a\).

parts.stem: Show that \(a=2\).
parts.hint: A probability density integrates to 1 over its entire interval. Integrate the given function from 0 to a, then solve the resulting equation.

keyPoints.note: Use the total area under the probability density on the interval from 0 to a.

steps.explain: The total probability must equal 1, so integrate the density from its lower endpoint 0 to its upper endpoint a.
Take the constant factor outside the integral and use the power rule.
Evaluate at the upper and lower limits and simplify.
Multiply both sides by 8 and take the positive cube root because a is an interval endpoint with a>0.

parts.stem: Find the exact value of the median of \(X\).
parts.hint: Set the cumulative probability from 0 to the median equal to one half.

keyPoints.text: Find the exact value of the median of \(X\).
keyPoints.note: Identify the given information in this exact phrase first, then connect it to the rule or calculation shown in the solution.

steps.explain: Let the median be m and set the area from 0 to m equal to 1/2.
Integrate and solve for m³.
Take the positive cube root because m lies in (0,2).

questions.stem: Consider the cumulative distribution function: \(F(x)=0\) for \((−\infty,0)\), \(F(x)=\sin(\frac{x}{2})\) for \([0,b]\), and \(F(x)=1\) for \((b,\infty)\). Find \(b\).
questions.hint: At the end of the middle interval, the cumulative probability must have reached 1.

keyPoints.note: Use continuity at the right endpoint: the middle formula must reach 1 when x=b.

steps.explain: A cumulative distribution function must join the middle formula to the constant value 1 at \(x=b\).
The first positive angle whose sine is 1 is \(\pi/2\). Thus the input angle \(b/2\) equals \(\pi/2\).
Multiply both sides by 2.
The matching choice is B.

questions.stem: The waiting time X (in minutes) for an ambulance after a 000 call has density \(f(x)=ax(10-x)\) for \(0\le x\le10\), and \(f(x)=0\) otherwise.

parts.stem: Show that the value of \(a\) is \(\frac3{500}\).
parts.hint: A probability density has total area 1 over its support; integrate from 0 to 10 and solve for a.

keyPoints.note: A probability density has total area 1 over its support; integrate from 0 to 10 and solve for a.

steps.explain: Because the density is zero outside 0≤x≤10, the total probability is the integral over this interval.
Expand the integrand and integrate term by term.
Evaluate at 10 and 0.
Solve for a.
Thus the normalized density uses the stated constant.

parts.stem: Find the cumulative distribution function.
parts.hint: Integrate the density from the lower support endpoint 0 to x, and attach the outside-support values.

keyPoints.note: Integrate the density from the lower support endpoint 0 to x and include the values outside the support.

steps.explain: For x<0, no waiting time values have accumulated, so F(x)=0. For 0≤x≤10, integrate the density.
Expand before integrating.
Substitute the limits and simplify.
For x>10, the entire density area has accumulated, so F(x)=1.
This piecewise function is the cumulative distribution.

parts.stem: Find the probability, as a decimal, that a person will have to wait more than 7 minutes.
parts.hint: Integrate the density over the tail from 7 to 10, or calculate 1−F(7).

keyPoints.note: Find the upper-tail probability by integrating from 7 to 10 or by calculating 1−F(7).

steps.explain: Waiting more than 7 minutes is the area under the density from 7 to the maximum wait 10.
An antiderivative is \((15x^2-x^3)/500\). Evaluate it at 10 and 7.
Subtract the accumulated probability up to 7 from 1.

questions.stem: People are given a maximum of six hours to complete a puzzle. The time spent on the puzzle, in hours, can be modelled using the continuous random variable X with probability density function \(f(x)= rac{Ax}{x^2+4}\) for 0≤x≤6, where A>0, and 0 otherwise. The graph of the probability density function is shown below. The graph has a local maximum.
questions.hint: Use total area 1 for the density constant. Differentiate to find the mode, integrate for the CDF probability, and use conditional probability for the IQ part.

parts.stem: Show that A = 2/ln 10.
parts.hint: The area under a probability density is 1. Integrate the given function from 0 to 6.

steps.explain: Set the total area under the density curve equal to 1.
Use u=x²+4, so du=2x dx. This turns the numerator x dx into du/2.
Integrate 1/u to ln u, then apply the limits.
Solve for A.

parts.stem: Show that the mode of X is two hours.
options: The density is maximised at x=2
The density is maximised at x=4
The density has no local maximum
parts.hint: The mode occurs where \(f'(x)=0\) at an interior maximum. Differentiate x/(x²+4) and check the turning point.

steps.explain: The constant A is positive, so it does not change where the curve reaches its maximum. Differentiate x/(x²+4) using the quotient rule.
Set the numerator equal to zero; the denominator is always positive. Within 0≤x≤6, the stationary point is x=2.
The derivative changes from positive to negative at x=2, so this is a maximum and therefore the mode.

keyPoints.note: The x-value where the density is greatest.

parts.stem: Show that P(X < 2) = log₁₀ 2.

Evaluate the limits and use the change-of-base definition of log base 10.

parts.stem: The Intelligence Quotient (IQ) scores of people are normally distributed with a mean of 100 and standard deviation of 15. It has been observed that the puzzle is generally completed more quickly by people with a high IQ. It is known that 80% of people with an IQ greater than 130 can complete the puzzle in less than two hours. A person chosen at random can complete the puzzle in less than two hours. What is the probability that this person has an IQ greater than 130? Give your answer correct to three decimal places.
parts.hint: Use conditional probability: P(IQ>130 | X<2)=P(X<2 | IQ>130)P(IQ>130)/P(X<2). A score of 130 is two standard deviations above 100.

From part c, the chance a randomly selected person finishes in under two hours is log₁₀2. For a high-IQ person, that chance is 0.80.
Apply Bayes’ rule, then round to three decimal places.

questions.stem: The probability density function, f, of a random variable X is given by \(f(x)= rac{3}{76}(x^2+1)\) for 0≤x≤k and 0 elsewhere.
questions.hint: Use area 1 to confirm the support endpoint. Then integrate the density over the interval x>2.

parts.stem: Explain why k = 4.

The density is zero at x=4.

parts.stem: Find P(X > 2). Give your answer correct to two decimal places.

questions.stem:
A spinner is biased as shown in the probability distribution below.

| \(x\) | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| \(P(X=x)\) | 0.2 | 0.15 | 0.08 | \(b\) | 0.12 | 0.10 |

Solve the following parts sequentially.

parts.stem: (a) Find the value of \(b\).

steps.explain: We begin by finding the value of b. Since all probabilities in the distribution must sum to exactly one, we set up an addition equation.

parts.stem: (b) Find \(P(1 < X \leq 4)\).

steps.explain: We calculate the probability of X being strictly between one and four (inclusive of four) by summing probabilities for two, three, and four.

parts.stem: (c) Find \(P(X \leq 4 \mid X > 1)\).

steps.explain: We calculate the conditional probability of X being less than or equal to four given X is greater than one.

parts.stem: (d) Find the expected value \(E(X)\).

steps.explain: We compute the expected value E(X) by summing the products of each outcome and its corresponding probability.

questions.hint: For (a): $\sum P=1$. For (c): $P(X\leq4|X>1)=\frac{P(1<X\leq4)}{P(X>1)}$. For (d)–(f): use standard formulas.

questions.stem: Kelly has been offered two part-time jobs at local furniture shops. At shop \\(X\\) she receives a retainer of \\(\$300\\) per week plus \\(\$200\\) for each lounge suite sold. At shop \\(Y\\) she receives \\(\$450\\) per week plus \\(\$100\\) per suite sold.\\n\\nPast weekly sales follow this probability distribution:\\n\\n| Suites sold | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |\\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|\\n| Probability | 0.1 | 0.2 | 0.5 | 0.15 | 0.04 | 0.01 |\\n\\nFind the expected number of lounge suites sold per week, rounded to the nearest whole number.

parts.stem: (a) Find the expected number of lounge suites sold per week. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

steps.explain: Apply the expected value formula by multiplying each outcome by its probability.
Round the resulting value to the nearest integer.

parts.stem: (b) Find the variance for this data.

steps.explain: First, we calculate the expected value of X squared by squaring each variable value and multiplying it by its probability.
Next, we calculate the variance by subtracting the square of the expected value from the expectation of X squared.

parts.stem: (c) Which furniture shop job should Kelly take? Justify your answer by referring to the expected weekly pay based on your result from part (a).
options: Kelly should take Shop \\(X\\) (expected pay of \\(\$700\\) vs \\(\$650\\) at Shop \\(Y\\))

Compare the two values and select the job that offers higher expected weekly earnings.

questions.hint: Use $\text{Var}(X) = E(X^2) - [E(X)]^2$. First calculate $E(X^2) = \sum x^2 \cdot P(X=x)$.

Apply variance formula by subtracting the square of the expected value from the expectation of X squared.

questions.stem:
Kelly is considering two furniture shop jobs.

- **Shop X** pays a weekly retainer of $\$300$ plus $\$200$ commission per sale.
- **Shop Y** pays a weekly retainer of $\$450$ plus $\$100$ commission per sale.

Let $X$ be the number of sales she makes in a week.

Using the expected value result $E(X) = 2$, which furniture shop job should Kelly take? Justify your answer by referring to her expected weekly pay.
options: Kelly should take Shop \(X\) (expected weekly pay of \(\$700\) vs \(\$650\) at Shop \(Y\))
Kelly should take Shop \(Y\) (expected weekly pay of \(\$650\) vs \(\$500\) at Shop \(X\))
Kelly should take Shop \(X\) (expected weekly pay of \(\$800\) vs \(\$750\) at Shop \(Y\))
Kelly should take Shop \(Y\) (expected weekly pay of \(\$650\) vs \(\$600\) at Shop \(X\))
questions.hint: Calculate the expected weekly pay at each shop using $E(\text{pay}) = \text{retainer} + \text{commission} \times E(X)$.
questions.solution: Shop $X$: $E(\text{pay}) = 300 + 200 \times 2 = \$700$. Shop $Y$: $E(\text{pay}) = 450 + 100 \times 2 = \$650$. Kelly should take Shop $X$ as her expected weekly pay is $\$700 > \$650$.

steps.explain: Calculate Shop X expected pay using E(X) = 2.
Calculate Shop Y expected pay.
Compare the two values and select the job that offers higher expected weekly earnings.

questions.stem: The probability density function for the continuous random variable \(X\) is \(f(x) = x^3-x+4\) for \(0 \le x \le 1\), and \(f(x)=0\) otherwise. What is \(E(X)\)?
questions.hint: Use \(E(X) = \displaystyle\int_0^1 x\,f(x)\,dx\).

steps.explain: Set up the integral for the expected value, multiplying \(x\) by the pdf and expanding.
Find the primitive of each term.
Evaluate at \(x=1\) (the lower limit gives 0).
Find a common denominator (15) and combine.

questions.stem: A continuous random variable \(X\) has a probability density function \(f(x) = 2x^3-x+a\) for \(0 \le x \le 1\), and \(f(x)=0\) otherwise.

parts.stem: (a) Find the value of \(a\) which makes \(f(x)\) a valid probability density function.
parts.hint: The total area under the pdf must equal 1: integrate \(f(x)\) from 0 to 1 and set it equal to 1.

steps.explain: Set the total integral of the pdf equal to 1.
Find the primitive and evaluate between the limits.
Set this equal to 1 and solve.

parts.stem: (b) Using \(a=1\), find the expected value and variance of \(X\).
parts.hint: Use \(E(X)=\int_0^1 x f(x)\,dx\) and \(\text{Var}(X)=\int_0^1 x^2f(x)\,dx - [E(X)]^2\).

steps.explain: Set up and evaluate the integral for \(E(X)\).
Evaluate at \(x=1\) and combine over a common denominator (30).
Set up and evaluate the integral for \(E(X^2)\).
Evaluate and subtract \([E(X)]^2\).

parts.stem: (a) Find \( a \) and \( b \).

steps.explain: Apply \( E(X)=\sum xP(X=x)=0.55 \), noting the \( x=0 \) term vanishes regardless of \( b \).

questions.stem: Let \( C \) be the event a family owns a cat and \( D \) be the event a family owns a dog. Given \( P(C)=\dfrac37 \), \( P(D\mid C')=\dfrac25 \), and \( P(D'\mid C)=\dfrac34 \).

parts.stem: (a) Which list correctly completes all six branch probabilities on the tree diagram?
parts.hint: Fill each branch using the given probability or its complement.
parts.solution: The correct branch probabilities are shown in option A.

steps.explain: The first set of branches splits on cat ownership, using the given \( P(C)=3/7 \) and its complement.
From a cat-owning family, \( P(D'|C)=3/4 \) is given, so \( P(D|C) \) is its complement.
From a non-cat-owning family, \( P(D|C')=2/5 \) is given directly, so \( P(D'|C') \) is its complement.

parts.stem: (b)(i) Find the probability that a family owns both a cat and a dog.
parts.hint: Multiply the probabilities along the cat-then-dog branch.

steps.explain: The event "owns both" corresponds to following the cat branch, then the dog-given-cat branch.
Substitute the known values (using \( P(D|C)=1/4 \) from part (a)).
Multiply the fractions. Pitfall: using \( P(D'|C)=3/4 \) instead of \( P(D|C)=1/4 \) here gives the wrong branch.

parts.stem: (b)(ii) Find the probability that a family owns at least one pet (a cat or a dog).
parts.hint: Use the complement of having neither pet.

steps.explain: "At least one pet" is the complement of "neither a cat nor a dog" — easier to compute via the complement.
Find \( P(C'\cap D') \) by following the no-cat branch then the no-dog-given-no-cat branch.
Subtract from 1. Pitfall: computing \( P(C'\cap D') \) but forgetting to subtract from 1 leaves the complement value itself as a wrong "answer".

questions.hint: At each split, the probabilities on the outgoing branches must add to 1.

keyPoints.note: Use complementary probabilities at every branch point.

questions.stem: Kelly has been offered two part-time jobs at local furniture shops. At furniture shop X she receives a retainer of $300 per week plus $200 for each lounge suite sold. At furniture shop Y she receives a retainer of $450 per week plus $100 for each lounge suite sold. Past weekly sales of lounge suites indicate the following probability distribution.

parts.stem: Find the expected number of lounge suites sold per week. Give your answer to the nearest whole.
parts.hint: Multiply each possible sales count by its probability and add the products.

keyPoints.note: Multiply each possible sales count by its probability, add, and round to the nearest whole number.

steps.explain: For a discrete random variable, the expected value is the probability-weighted sum of possible outcomes.
